Brazil: the real breaks through 6 to the dollar, and lawmakers swiftly pass Lula's savings plan by 353 votes to 128 without changing a comma

Overnight from November 23 to 24, Brazil's Chamber of Deputies passed the Lula government's savings plan, a few hours after the real fell beyond 6 reais to the dollar. All ten amendments were rejected: the bill goes straight to the president for signature [1][2][3].
The main text, complementary bill PLP 299/2026, was approved by 353 votes to 128, with five abstentions [2][4]. As a complementary law, it needed at least 257 votes out of 513 [4].

Lawmakers then rejected the ten amendments tabled, including those from the Liberal Party (PL, right), which voted against [3][5]. No changes: the bill does not return to the Senate and goes to presidential sanction as the Senate passed it [3].
The plan allows the government to freeze spending even when the fiscal target has already been met, and doubles, from 10% to 20%, the cut in tax breaks granted to companies and sectors [3][5].
The expected impact varies by source: up to 60 billion reais (about $10 billion) next year according to AP, up to 56.1 billion reais on the 2027 balance according to other estimates [6][5].
According to Bloomberg, the vote came a few hours after the real crossed the closely watched threshold of 6 reais to the dollar [1].
The Senate passed the bill last week by 69 votes to 2, after rejecting three changes that would have narrowed its scope [4][6].

Key takeaway: by pushing the vote through quickly and without changes, Lula wants to reassure investors who are selling the Brazilian currency. The 6-reais-to-the-dollar threshold is symbolic: it shows that markets doubt the country's ability to keep its finances in order [1][7].

Brazil is expected to end 2026 with a primary deficit (before interest payments on the debt) of about 52 billion reais, or $8.8 billion, according to the Chamber's news agency [4]. The 2026 elections were costly for public finances [6].

Analysts criticize the plan for relying more on extra revenue, by trimming tax loopholes, than on genuine spending cuts. That doubt has weighed on Brazilian assets in recent days, including the real [7].

What comes next will play out in the markets: if the real does not recover, imported inflation will rise and the central bank, which has already sold dollars to support the currency, may have to act again.

A weak real makes Brazil cheaper for you if you travel there, but makes imported goods, including European ones, more expensive for Brazilians. French companies with a strong presence in Brazil, such as in retail or energy, earn less there once their profits are converted into euros.

Argentina: the vote on Milei's 2027 budget is pushed back to Thursday, with lawmakers still missing to open the session, while “country risk” falls 30 points

Javier Milei's government is now aiming for Thursday, November 26, to get its 2027 budget through the Chamber of Deputies. It still lacks allies to reach the quorum of 129 members. On Monday, “country risk” fell back to 1,035 points, after a yearly high on Friday [1][2][4][5].

The session was first scheduled for Wednesday, November 25; it is now targeted for Thursday the 26th, with a debate that could last around twenty hours [2][3]. On the same day, the Senate is due to consider a political reform that suspends the mandatory primaries (PASO) [3].

Milei's party, La Libertad Avanza, has 94 deputies and hopes for 21 votes from allies: not enough for the 129 members present needed to open the session [2][3]. Last week, it had already failed to reach a quorum [3].

It must win over the Provincias Unidas bloc (18 deputies), linked to governors Martín Llaryora (Córdoba) and Maximiliano Pullaro (Santa Fe), which is demanding funds, public works and money for universities [3][4]. The government's “political table” meets this Tuesday at 1 p.m. to seal agreements [4].

On November 17 the bill received a favorable committee report, with 27 signatures [6]. It forecasts 4% growth in 2027, 18% inflation for the year and an official dollar at 1,847.60 pesos in December 2027 [6].

On Monday, a public holiday in Argentina, “country risk,” the gap between the rate at which Argentina borrows and that of the United States, fell 30 points to 1,035 points, lifted by the rebound on Wall Street [1][7]. It had closed Friday at 1,070 points, its highest of 2026, compared with about 400 in early July [5].
Key takeaway: a passed budget is a signal creditors are waiting for. Without it, Milei would face markets in a weakened position, as they already doubt his ability to repay [5][8].

Argentina must pay nearly $17 billion to its bondholders in 2027, according to the Financial Times as cited by the Buenos Aires Herald [8]. Argentine dollar bonds now price in only about a 45% chance of Milei being re-elected in 2027, according to the firm FMyA [8].
The timetable is tight: Congress's ordinary sessions end on November 30 [6]. The governors know this and are raising the stakes, because their deputies are the key to the quorum [3][4].
If the budget passes the Chamber, it will still have to be considered by the Senate, where time is short [6].

If you follow emerging markets or hold a bond fund that includes them, Argentina remains one of the riskiest countries: a budget failure could revive the slide in its bonds. Spanish banks, which have a strong presence there, are also exposed to these shocks.

United States: before Democrats take over Congress, Trump bars federal contractors from answering investigators without notifying the White House, or risk losing their contracts

In an executive order signed Friday, Donald Trump requires all companies working for the federal government to notify the White House before handing information to Congress. Democrats, who will take control of both chambers in January, denounce an “illegal” measure designed to stifle their investigations [1][2][3].

The order is titled “Protecting Executive Privileges and Improving the Efficiency of Federal Procurement.” It immediately requires federal contractors and their subcontractors to report to the White House any “pending or future” request from Congress [2][3].

Companies that do not comply risk having their contracts terminated and being suspended from any future work with the federal government [2]. They must also withhold documents that the administration deems covered by “executive privilege” [2][4].
The text asserts that Congress may request information from the executive branch only for a “valid legislative purpose” that does not encroach on the president's core functions [2].

It builds on a November 16 memo from White House counsel Will Scharf: agencies must obtain his approval before an official agrees to testify before a committee [2][3]. In a letter, Scharf reminded Democrats that they are not yet in the majority and cannot demand anything [2].
Democrat Jamie Raskin called the measure “totally unprecedented and plainly illegal”; Robert Garcia called it a “flagrant attack on Congress's constitutional right to oversee” the government [2].
According to CNN, the standoff is “catching fire”: Trump is trying to limit who, how and what Democrats will be able to investigate, and investigators are making this order their first target [1].

Key takeaway: congressional oversight of the government often goes through private companies (subcontractors, vendors, advisers). By threatening them with the loss of their contracts, the White House is cutting off a major source of information even before Democrats have subpoena power [1][2][5].

Democrats, who won the November elections for the House and the Senate, want to investigate conflicts of interest, federal contracts, immigration enforcement and the handling of the Jeffrey Epstein case [1][2]. They have also sent letters asking for documents on Trump's construction projects in Washington to be preserved, after whistleblower warnings about destruction; the White House calls it “harassment” [6].

Time is on the executive's side: according to lawyers cited by CNN, Congress would have only 12 to 18 months for its investigations to carry political weight before the 2028 presidential campaign, and the administration is expected to play for time [5].
The courts can settle these disputes over Congress's investigative power, but a legal battle would also take time [2].

For you, the stakes are indirect but real: a US president under less oversight can more freely decide on tariffs, sanctions or military commitments that affect Europe. French companies under contract with the US government could also find themselves caught between the White House and congressional investigators.

Egypt: amid the Hormuz crisis, Iraq considers sending 10 million barrels of oil to Cairo, where its prime minister is making his first visit

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi was received on Monday, November 23, in Cairo by Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, on his first official visit to Egypt. Energy, trade, defense and water were on the agenda, as Baghdad considers a proposal to deliver about 10 million barrels of oil [1][2][3].
The two leaders discussed cooperation in energy, investment, trade and defense, as well as Gaza, Yemen and security in the Red Sea [1][3].
Iraq is considering a proposal to supply Egypt with about 10 million barrels of oil [4]. No signed contract was announced at the end of the meeting [3][4].
The visit coincides with the fourth session of the Iraqi-Egyptian Joint Higher Committee, which oversees agreements and protocols between the two countries [2][3].
Abdel Fattah al-Sisi called Iraq's stability a “fundamental pillar of Arab national security” [3].

The two countries presented themselves as “downstream” states on major rivers (the Nile for Egypt, the Tigris and the Euphrates for Iraq) and called for respect for international law on shared watercourses [3].
Trade between the two countries reached $1.1 billion in 2024 [2].

Key takeaway: Egypt is looking for energy sources and fresh money, and Iraq, a major oil producer, is seeking closer ties with Cairo: 10 million barrels are under consideration, with no contract signed at this stage [1][3][4].

Cairo needs foreign currency: on November 18, the IMF and Egypt reached a staff-level agreement on the eighth and final review of their aid program, which could unlock about $2.3 billion if the IMF Executive Board approves it [5][6]. The program, which was extended, ends on December 15, 2026 [5].

According to the IMF, Egypt beat its end-September targets for tax revenue and the primary surplus (the budget balance excluding interest on the debt), with 5.1% growth in fiscal year 2025/2026 [5]. This model student therefore needs to keep its finances under control, and oil supplied by a friendly country would ease its bill.

Egypt controls the Suez Canal, through which part of the goods traded between Asia and Europe pass. A country that secures its energy and finances means one less risk for this trade route, and therefore for the prices of what you buy in France.

Côte d'Ivoire: the first German president in Abidjan in 40 years, Steinmeier hails a “central partner” and nearly €1 billion in projects

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier was received on Monday, November 23, by Alassane Ouattara in Abidjan. It is the first visit by a German head of state to Côte d'Ivoire in about 40 years. On the agenda: nearly €970 million in cooperation, security in the face of terrorism, and climate [1][2][4].

Having arrived on Sunday, November 22, Frank-Walter Steinmeier was welcomed with military honors at the presidential palace on Monday, before talks, a joint press conference and lunch with Alassane Ouattara [1][2].

According to the German agency dpa, no German head of state had visited the country in 40 years [1]. Ivorian media even speak of a first in 43 years; Alassane Ouattara called the visit “historic” [4][5].
The Ivorian president put the German economic cooperation under way in the country at €968.62 million, implemented by the public agencies KfW (development bank) and GIZ (technical cooperation) [4].

Steinmeier described Côte d'Ivoire as a central partner for Germany in West Africa [3]. He was due to visit a vocational school and the International Academy for Combating Terrorism in Jacqueville, whose work he praised [1][4].
He was made Grand Cross of the National Order of the Republic of Côte d'Ivoire [4].
The trip lasts four days: after Abidjan, Steinmeier is due to open a German-African business summit in Accra (Ghana), then meet Kenyan President William Ruto in Nairobi [1].
On the same day, the president of the EBRD, a European public development bank, was also in Abidjan to open an office there [6].
Key takeaway: Germany, Europe's largest economy, is sending its head of state to a country it had not visited at that level in 40 years, and presents it as its central partner in West Africa [1][3].

According to the German presidency, the trip is meant to honor three “partner” countries in defending a rules-based international order, and to encourage German companies to invest more on the African continent [1].

Security is at the heart of the relationship: the two presidents discussed climate and security, and Steinmeier praised the work of the International Academy for Combating Terrorism in Jacqueville, near Abidjan [4].
The next step is already set: the sixth session of the joint cooperation commission between the two countries is due to be held on November 26 and 27 [4].

Côte d'Ivoire is a historic partner of France. Seeing Germany invest nearly €1 billion there shows that competition among Europeans for West Africa is accelerating: for French companies based in Abidjan, that means both more rivals and more funded projects.

North Korea: with no meeting with Trump, Kim Jong-un personally receives ten ambassadors, a first in more than 30 years, and touts his country's “sovereignty”

Kim Jong-un personally received the credentials of ten new ambassadors, including Russia's, the official KCNA agency announced on Monday, November 23. It is an unprecedented gesture in more than 30 years, a few days after Donald Trump left Asia without meeting him [1][3][4].
The ceremony was held on Sunday, November 22, at the Workers' Party headquarters in Pyongyang; KCNA reported it on Monday [3][4].

The ten ambassadors represent Russia, Sweden, Indonesia, Vietnam, Brazil, the Czech Republic, India, the Philippines, Thailand and Bangladesh [4]. Kim wore a suit and tie, with his foreign minister, Choe Son-hui, at his side [2].

According to the Russian agency TASS, as reported by the South Korean agency Yonhap, this is the first time in more than 30 years that a North Korean leader has personally received an ambassador: since the era of Kim Jong-il, that task fell to the president of the Presidium of the Supreme People's Assembly [4].

The change stems from a constitutional revision in March that gives this power to the president of the State Affairs Commission, a post held by Kim [4]. The Russian ambassador, Andrei Podyolyshev, appointed in late July, has been in post since September [4].
“The DPRK is ready to strengthen ties of friendship and cooperation with all countries that respect the sovereignty of our state,” Kim said [2].
Donald Trump left Asia after the APEC summit in Shenzhen without seeing Kim, even though he had hinted that a meeting was possible [1][2].
Key takeaway: Kim is responding to silence with staging. By personally receiving ten diplomats, he shows that he does not need Washington to matter on the international stage [1][2].
For South Korean analyst Lim Eul-chul, quoted by AFP via RTÉ, the gesture marks a shift toward a “multipolar” diplomacy based on sovereignty [2]. Russia tops the list of ambassadors received [3][4].

This message comes as the nuclear program advances: on November 18, the director of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Rafael Grossi, said that an extension of the Yongbyon uranium enrichment plant, begun in mid-September, was completed from the outside by late October, a source of “serious concern” [5].
The IAEA can only monitor from afar: it has had no inspectors in the country since 2009 and relies on satellite imagery [5].

North Korea may seem far away, but its rapprochement with Russia, which is at war with Ukraine, directly affects Europe's security. And every advance in its nuclear program makes a deal harder, which fuels tensions in Asia, a key region for the chips and electronics you buy.

India-Nepal: for young Prime Minister Balendra Shah's first visit, Modi offers a record $1.6 billion in aid and a train to Janakpur

Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah, 35, wrapped up his first official visit to India on Monday, November 23. Narendra Modi offered him an aid package of 24,000 crore (240 billion) Nepalese rupees, or about $1.6 billion, the largest ever granted to Nepal, and eight agreements were signed [1][2][3].
Balendra Shah was in India on November 22 and 23, at Narendra Modi's invitation, for his first bilateral visit as head of government [1][2].

The development cooperation package amounts to 24,000 crore Nepalese rupees, about $1.6 billion (15,000 crore Indian rupees) [2][3]. Indian Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri called it the largest package ever given to Nepal [2].

Eight memorandums of understanding were signed: space research, health, Ayurvedic medicine, civil service training, urban planning, satellite communications, police cooperation, and livestock and fisheries [1].

The two leaders launched the Sarayu-Kamala Express train between Ayodhya, in India, and Janakpur, in Nepal, and opened a road bridge between Dharchula and Darchula, on either side of the border [2][4].
India is accepting two-way traffic on the Bhairahawa-Lucknow air route, but other Nepalese requests for airspace access remain unanswered [2].

A joint document, “Viksit Bharat and Samunnat Nepal” (Developed India, Prosperous Nepal), sets out a broader vision than the agreements signed [2]. Balendra Shah invited Narendra Modi to Nepal and called on Indian investors to come [3].
Key takeaway: India is paying the price to keep Nepal, squeezed between it and China, in its camp [2][5].

Kathmandu was asking for up to $2 billion in economic aid, according to the Kathmandu Post [5]. New Delhi is not granting all of it, but comes close, with what The Wire describes as its largest financial commitment to its neighbor [2].

Several issues remain open: rupee loans, new air routes, rail extension and revision of the trade treaty between the two countries [5]. Nepalese experts advised rebuilding trust before arriving with a wish list [6].
Nepal depends heavily on India for its trade and fuel. For a leader who came to power very young, returning home with record aid and new links is a first political success.

Nepal is far away, but this tug-of-war for influence between India and China is playing out across South Asia. It weighs on trade routes and major infrastructure projects in which European companies are also trying to gain a foothold.

Australia
Australia: Google and Meta face fines of up to 5% of their global revenue, and users will be able to sue them

Anthony Albanese's Australian government reached a deal with the Greens on Tuesday, November 24, to pass its “digital duty of care.” Platforms will have to prevent online harms or face fines of up to 5% of their global revenue, and victims will be able to take them to court [1][2].

Communications Minister Anika Wells announced that groups such as Google and Meta could pay up to 5% of their global revenue; the original bill capped the fine at 109 million Australian dollars, about 72 million US dollars [1].

Platforms will have to actively check for and prevent foreseeable harms to their users [1]. The bill covers social networks, search engines, app stores and generative artificial intelligence services; small-business sites deemed low-risk are exempt [2].
Australians gain the right to sue a platform that fails in this duty, and the internet regulator's powers are expanded to have fake nude images created by AI (“nudify”) taken down [1].
The conservative opposition opposes the bill in the name of free speech; the government therefore needed the Greens, who were calling for heavier penalties and a right to redress for victims [2][3].
Already passed by the House of Representatives, the bill is due to go to the Senate this week; it is expected to be passed by next Thursday, the last sitting week of the year [1][2].
The Digital Industry Group, which represents the platforms, criticizes the bill; it had not seen the new version when it was approached [2].
Key takeaway: with a penalty calculated on global revenue, the fine goes from a few tens of millions to potentially billions of dollars for the tech giants [1][2].

The companies say they share the goal of better protecting children, but most oppose the bill because it leaves officials leeway to decide what is “harmful”; they fear having to remove too much content [1][2].
Australia is already a pioneer: in 2024 it passed a law setting a minimum age for using social media [4]. This new bill goes further, by making platforms responsible for what happens on them.

The model resembles the EU's Digital Services Act (DSA), which also provides for fines as a percentage of global revenue. Australia is thus joining the regulation camp, while Washington criticizes this kind of rule.

What is decided in Australia often serves as a test for other countries. If Google, Meta or TikTok have to change their moderation tools there, those changes often end up applying elsewhere, including to your account in France.

news.2026-11-24-israel-eisenkot-coalitio: Israel: four weeks after the elections, Eisenkot is preparing a surprise vote to form his government, even if it means relying on the Arab parties

Nearly a month after the October 27 legislative elections, Gadi Eisenkot still has no majority to replace Benjamin Netanyahu. According to the Israeli press, he wants to announce a coalition by surprise and have it voted on within 24 to 48 hours, while his ally Naftali Bennett disagrees over the ultimatum to give Likud [1][2][3].
Eisenkot's four-party bloc won 48 of the 120 seats; Netanyahu's allies have 53, including 13 for the ultra-Orthodox parties, and the Arab parties 19 [4].

The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party (7 seats) has refused to back Netanyahu and is negotiating with Eisenkot [4]. An Eisenkot ally, Matan Kahana, has already been elected Speaker of the Knesset [4].

According to public broadcaster Kan, Eisenkot plans to announce that he has found a way to form a government, then hold the confidence vote within 24 to 48 hours to avoid maneuvers and defections [2][3].
On November 23, the Times of Israel reported that Eisenkot and Naftali Bennett were divided over the idea of setting a deadline for Likud in talks on a unity government [1].
If no broad coalition is possible, Eisenkot has said he would form an “emergency government” [5]; he could then govern as a minority with the support of the Arab parties [4].
In the meantime, Benjamin Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister [4].
Key takeaway: for the first time in years, Netanyahu could lose power, but his rival does not yet have the 61 seats needed to govern [4].

The math is tight: even with United Torah Judaism's 7 seats, Eisenkot's bloc would reach only 55 seats [4]. Hence the idea of support from the Arab parties, a rare and highly contested option in Israel.

The change would not only be political. Eisenkot, a former chief of staff, has said that Iran does not pose an immediate threat requiring military action, contrary to Netanyahu [6]. His arrival could change Israel's line in the regional war.
Likud can still play for time and poach lawmakers: that is why Eisenkot wants a quick vote, at a moment of his choosing [3].

Who governs Israel weighs on the war with Iran, and therefore on the Strait of Hormuz and the price of oil. A government less inclined to strike Tehran could, over time, make de-escalation in the Gulf easier.
